sentences.text: A short, blade-like crest sits beneath the front of the lower jaws.
Rodrigues and Kellner noted that the sockets for the teeth are raised higher than the roof of the mouth and the edge of the lower jaw.
The sockets at the very front of the jaws measure no more than four millimeters across.
The gap separating these sockets is equal to the width of the sockets themselves.
A ridge runs along the center line of the palate.
A crest is also present on the lower section of the lower jaw.
The front of the jaw margin holds about six tooth sockets for every three centimeters of length.
This species is defined by a crested snout, a rounded snout tip, a rounded lower jaw front, and diverging front tooth sockets.
Bowerbank estimated the wingspan of this creature to be between 2.4 and 2.7 meters.
Earlier, Bowerbank had guessed the span of a related species was roughly eight to nine feet.
James Scott Bowerbank named and described the species in 1846 using fossils from a limestone quarry near Maidstone in Kent.
In 1914, Reginald Walter Hooley moved the species into a new genus called Lonchodectes, which translates to 'the spear-biter'.
The original specimen of Lonchodraco giganteus was discovered in the Chalk Formation.
Researchers treat Lonchodraco as a group defined by unique shared features that separate it from relatives.
In the species Lonchodraco machaerorhynchus, a high crest exists in the lower zone of the lower jaw.
Towards the rear, the profile of this crest curves upward in Lonchodraco machaerorhynchus.
Behind the crest, a depression appears on the lower part of the jaw in Lonchodraco machaerorhynchus.
The groove in the center of the upper part of the lower jaw symphysis is deep in Lonchodraco machaerorhynchus.
Additionally, Lonchodraco machaerorhynchus has a density of 4.5 teeth for every three centimeters of the jaw margin.
A high border is found on the midline of the palate in Lonchodraco(?) microdon.
The distance between the tooth sockets exceeds their diameters in Lonchodraco(?) microdon.

Lonchodraco(?) microdon possesses a unique set of traits: it lacks a snout crest, has a rounded snout tip profile, a convex palate midline and jaw margins, and a density of 4.5 teeth per three centimeters of jaw margin.
Pterodactylus giganteus serves as the type species for Lonchodraco, resulting in the full name Lonchodraco giganteus.
Two other species formerly placed in Lonchodectes were transferred to Lonchodraco, becoming Lonchodraco machaerorhynchus and Lonchodraco(?) microdon.
The question mark in the name Lonchodraco(?) microdon signals that authors are uncertain about the correctness of this assignment.
In 2013, Rodrigues and Kellner assigned Lonchodraco to the family Lonchodraconidae, which they defined as containing only Lonchodraco.
Rodrigues and Kellner also stated that Lonchodraco is the sole member of the family Lonchodraconidae.
Later studies by Pêgas et al. and Holgado & Pêgas recovered Lonchodraco within Lonchodraconidae as the sister taxon to Ikrandraco.
Lonchodraco was a pterodactyloid pterosaur that lived during the Early and Late Cretaceous in southern England.
The animal lived from the Valanginian to the Turonian, between 137.05 and 89.8 million years ago.
Averianov (2020) debated the classification of Lonchodraco, assigning L. machaerorhynchus to the genus Ikrandraco and declaring L. microdon a junior synonym.

The type specimen of Ornithocheirus oweni was referred to Lonchodraco(?) microdon in the same study where Lonchodraco was named, following David Unwin's 2001 conclusions, and this species might therefore be a more modern synonym.
